_comment: Example operator config for the legal pages. Copy this file to your deployment directory (NOT into the public repo!) as 'operator.json' and fill in your real values. It is deployment-specific data; note that the deployed operator.json is nevertheless listed in the signed manifest, so changing it requires a re-sign. Only strings; no HTML or code. Legal placeholders contain example text for an Italian operator and MUST be adapted to your jurisdiction, including NIS2 classification, DSA registration, and other regulatory obligations. This is NOT legal advice.
OPERATOR_DPA_NAME: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali
OPERATOR_HOSTING_NOTE: The virtual machine is located in a data centre within the European Economic Area and the Controller has accepted the provider's data-processing terms in accordance with Article 28 GDPR. If the provider is established outside the EEA, describe here the transfer mechanism relied on (for example the Standard Contractual Clauses incorporated in the data-processing agreement).
OPERATOR_LOG_RETENTION: The application writes no access log, and its reverse proxy is configured not to write access or error logs. Apart from start-up notices about its own configuration, the application writes only error messages to its log output, and those are written so as not to contain IP addresses, User-Agent strings, room identifiers or request metadata.
OPERATOR_HOSTING_PROVIDER_LOG_NOTE: Independently of the Controller, the hosting provider may retain infrastructure-level network logs (for example netflow or connection metadata) for its own purposes, as an autonomous controller under its own privacy policy. That processing is outside the Controller's control.
OPERATOR_LIABILITY_LOCAL_LAW_NOTE: This limitation applies to the fullest extent permitted under Italian law, including Articles 1218 and 1229 of the Italian Civil Code.
OPERATOR_DPO_NOTE: Based on the current scale and nature of this Service, no Data Protection Officer is believed to be required under Article 37 GDPR. This assessment will be reviewed if the Service's scope or data processing activities change materially.
OPERATOR_LEGAL_CLASSIFICATION_NOTE: The Service does not connect with, or enable communications using, publicly assigned numbering resources. To the extent that the Service qualifies as an electronic communications service under Directive (EU) 2018/1972 and Legislative Decree 259/2003 as amended, its characteristics are those of a number-independent interpersonal communications service (NI-ICS). Under Article 11(2) of Legislative Decree 259/2003, NI-ICS are not subject to the general-authorisation requirement. That provision concerns the general authorisation only: it does not mean that no other obligation under electronic-communications law applies to the Service. Whether a service offered free of charge by a private individual is an electronic communications service at all, a notion the law ties to services normally provided for remuneration, has not been determined. This paragraph states the Operator's understanding; no authority has confirmed it.
OPERATOR_LEGAL_FRAMEWORK_NOTE: This note records how the Operator currently understands the legal position of the Service, and keeps apart what is established from what is not. Verified in the published source code: the Service relays end-to-end encrypted messages in real time between browsers that are connected at the same moment; it does not connect with publicly assigned numbering resources; it has no user accounts, no message queue for absent participants and no access log. Declared by the Operator about the deployment, and not verifiable from the source code: the Service is run free of charge by a private individual, without advertising and without any other form of monetisation, on a single virtual server whose provider and location are stated in the Privacy Policy, and during the beta it can be reached only with a shared password. Interpretation, not settled: Directive (EU) 2018/1972 and the Italian Electronic Communications Code (Legislative Decree 259/2003 as replaced by Legislative Decree 207/2021) define an electronic communications service, and an interpersonal communications service, as a service normally provided for remuneration. Being free of charge does not settle that point. The Court of Justice has held that remuneration need not be paid by the recipients of a service, and that a service offered free of charge in order to advertise the provider's own goods or services is an economic activity (judgment of 15 September 2016, Mc Fadden, C-484/14, paragraphs 41 and 42); recital 16 of Directive (EU) 2018/1972 extends the notion of remuneration to cases in which the user is exposed to advertising or gives access to personal data, the IP address included. Those texts do not address a service with no economic purpose at all, and the Operator knows of no decision or guidance that does. Whether the Service is an electronic communications service is therefore recorded here as an open question. If it is one, its characteristics are those of a number-independent interpersonal communications service, and Article 11(2) of the Code leaves such services outside the general-authorisation regime; that concerns the general authorisation only. Assistance to the judicial authorities: Article 57 of the Code places interception-related duties on entities authorised to operate public electronic communications networks and services, while Article 3 of the Ministerial Decree of 28 December 2017 extends mandatory assistance to anyone who provides electronic communications services or applications, including over networks that are not their own. Whether and how those provisions reach the Service has not been determined and is not asserted here either way. Data retention: Article 132 of the Privacy Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003) requires providers of publicly available electronic communications services to retain traffic data. The Operator's reading is that the general retention duty does not reach a service that generates no traffic or subscriber records; that reading has not been confirmed by any authority, and the Italian provisions still refer to older definitions. Orders to preserve specific data that the Operator actually holds are a separate matter and can be addressed to the Operator. Confirmed: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 applies to the personal data the Service processes, and lawful orders of the competent authorities must be complied with within the limits of the data held. Nothing in this note states that an obligation does not apply; where the position is uncertain it is recorded as uncertain.
OPERATOR_JUDICIAL_COOPERATION_NOTE: The Operator cooperates with the competent judicial and administrative authorities and complies with legally valid requests and orders, within the limits of the data actually held and of the obligations that apply. Verified in the published source code: encryption is end-to-end between browsers; the room link carries key material in its URL fragment, which browsers do not send to the server; session keys are derived in the browsers; the server relays ciphertext and keeps no message store, no access log and no record of who communicated with whom. Consequences: the Operator cannot provide message content in the clear or a record of past connections, because neither is held. Data that exist only in memory while a room or a connection is live (room identifiers and settings, connection identifiers, the addresses of open connections) are not written anywhere by the application, and the Service has no tool for extracting them; whether and how they could be produced in response to an order would have to be assessed case by case. The Operator can confirm the existence of the Service, how it is run, and any correspondence it holds. This describes what exists to be provided. It is not a claim that the absence of records releases the Operator from any order. Electronic evidence: Regulation (EU) 2023/1543 on European Production and Preservation Orders applies from 18 August 2026 to service providers offering services in the Union, a notion that again turns on the open question described in the legal classification note. The Regulation creates no general duty to retain data and concerns data stored at the time an order is received; an addressee that does not hold the requested data must tell the issuing authority so without undue delay, and Italian law (Legislative Decree 188/2026) attaches fines to failing to do that. Directive (EU) 2023/1544 and Legislative Decree 216/2025 require service providers with legal personality to designate an establishment for receiving such orders; the Operator is a natural person and reads that duty as not addressed to it, a reading no authority has confirmed. The languages the Operator accepts at its published addresses are stated in the Terms of Service; the language in which such orders are transmitted is governed by the Regulation itself.
OPERATOR_CASE_LAW_NOTE: This note is background only. The Italian Court of Cassation has decided several cases about messages exchanged on the Sky ECC encrypted platform. The Joint Chambers (Sezioni Unite, judgments no. 23755 and no. 23756, hearing of 29 February 2024, filed on 14 June 2024) dealt with the conditions under which data obtained by a foreign authority and transmitted to Italy through a European Investigation Order may be used in Italian proceedings, and held that the matter is governed by the rules on the circulation of evidence between proceedings (Articles 238 and 270 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) and not by Article 234-bis. Earlier decisions of the First Chamber (no. 6363 and no. 19082 of 2023) are cited in those judgments as having applied Article 234-bis. Commentary attributes to the first of them the statement that, in an end-to-end encrypted system, not even the operator of the service knows the keys or the content; the Operator has not verified that passage in the text of the judgment. These decisions concern the admissibility of evidence obtained abroad. They do not rule on what a service provider must or need not do, and they are not relied on here for any conclusion about the obligations of the Service.
OPERATOR_LEGAL_RISKS_NOTE: Points the Operator keeps under review. They are listed as open questions, not as conclusions. (1) Mandatory assistance. Article 57 of the Electronic Communications Code refers, for interception-related duties, to entities authorised to operate public networks and services, but its paragraph 6 allows a ministerial decree to identify obliged subjects among those who provide electronic communications services or applications over networks that are not their own, and Article 3 of the Ministerial Decree of 28 December 2017 already extends mandatory assistance to such providers. Article 4(1)(a) of that decree requires assistance 'regardless of the network technology employed or the type of access network', wording that concerns the type of network and does not mention encryption. The Operator has found no provision of Italian law that expressly requires a provider to decrypt communications or to hand over encryption keys; that search was limited to the Code and to the 2017 decree, and it is not a finding that no such provision exists. (2) Scanning of private communications. The interim derogation in Regulation (EU) 2021/1232 expired on 3 April 2026. Regulation (EU) 2026/1881 introduced a new temporary derogation, applicable until 3 April 2028, which by its Article 1(3) does not apply to interpersonal communications protected by end-to-end encryption. The proposal for a Child Sexual Abuse Regulation (2022/0155(COD)) had not been adopted when this note was last reviewed, in November 2026, and was still being negotiated between the institutions; its final content could affect end-to-end encrypted services. (3) Classification. The questions recorded in the legal classification, NIS2, Digital Services Act and cooperation notes all turn on whether a free service with no economic purpose is a service 'normally provided for remuneration', and, for NIS2, on what 'publicly available' means for a password-gated beta. A public opening, any form of funding, or a decision or guidance on these points would require those notes to be reviewed.
OPERATOR_NIS2_NOTE: Whether the NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555), transposed in Italy by Legislative Decree 138/2024, applies to the Service has not been determined. Established from the texts: the Directive and the Italian decree apply, regardless of size, to providers of publicly available electronic communications services (Article 2(2)(a)(i) of the Directive; Article 3(5)(b) of the decree); the decree covers natural persons as well as legal persons; entities in scope register on the platform of the national authority (ACN) between 1 January and 28 February of each year; and an entity in scope under the size-independent rule that is smaller than a medium-sized enterprise would be an important entity, not an essential one. Open: the Directive takes its definition of electronic communications service from Directive (EU) 2018/1972, so the question whether a free service with no economic purpose is such a service (see the legal classification note) arises here as well; and the Operator has found no definition or guidance on whether a service that can be reached only with a beta password is 'publicly available'. Current position: the Operator has not concluded that the Service is in scope, has not registered, and does not describe the Service as an essential or important entity. The question has to be answered before any public opening; if the answer is that the Directive applies, its registration, security and incident-notification duties apply with it. Independently of that question, the security measures in place are: end-to-end encryption of message content, Argon2id hashing of the access password, HMAC-signed CSRF tokens, proof-of-work and rate limiting against abuse, automatic room expiry, and a containerised deployment without root privileges and with all Linux capabilities dropped, all of which can be checked in the published source code and container configuration, together with TLS for transport, which is a property of the deployment.
OPERATOR_DSA_NOTE: Whether the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) applies to the Service has not been determined. It applies to intermediary services, which are information society services, that is, services normally provided for remuneration (Article 3(a) and (g); recital 5). The Service is free of charge, carries no advertising, is not monetised, and is run by a natural person in a personal capacity. That does not by itself place it outside the definition: the Court of Justice has held that the remuneration need not come from the recipient (Mc Fadden, C-484/14, paragraphs 41 and 42) and that such services are covered in so far as they represent an economic activity (Papasavvas, C-291/13, paragraph 28). Neither judgment, nor any guidance known to the Operator, addresses a service with no economic purpose. If the Regulation does apply, the Service has the characteristics of a 'mere conduit' (Article 3(g)(i); recital 29 mentions interpersonal communications services), because it transmits information provided by the recipient and keeps it only in an automatic, intermediate and transient manner for the purpose of the transmission; it would not be a hosting service or an online platform (recital 14). In that case Articles 11, 12 and 14 would apply, since they contain no exemption for small providers, while the annual report of Article 15(1) is not owed by micro or small enterprises (Article 15(2)). Whatever the answer, the Operator publishes contact addresses for authorities and for users, states the languages accepted there (Italian and English), and publishes its terms and the way reports are handled. This is done as a matter of practice; it is not a statement that every requirement that may apply is met.
